newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria's Abacha looks certain to seek presidency.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria's Abacha looks certain to seek presidency.

text.p: Nigerian military ruler General Sani Abacha will most likely contest next year's presidential poll, analysts said on Thursday, citing remarks he made in a rare interview with a U.S. newspaper.

The 53-year-old infantry general, who seldom gives interviews, told the Washington Times newspaper this week he had not considered whether he should stand in the election meant to fully restore democracy to Nigeria.

"Now it appears beyond doubt that General Abacha will run," wrote Thisday newspaper's political editor Ezuiche Ubani, a leading commentator on Abacha's programme to transfer from military to civilian rule.
"It is not what Abacha said in the interview that is news, it is what he did not say...he failed to rule himself out of political contention."
Political analysts agree that by not ruling out his candidature, Abacha was tactically saying he would contest.
"Everything appears to point that he will run," said A.P.T. Okpakpo, a former commissioner in the old Bendel state in midwestern Nigeria.
The issue of whether or not Abacha genuinely intends to hand over to a democratically-elected president has dogged the transition to civil rule programme he unveiled in 1995.

Abacha has faced problems since November, 1993 when he seized power in the anarchy unleashed by the annulment of a presidential vote in June deemed to have been won by millionaire businessman Moshood Abiola.
He banned all political activity, cracked down on opponents and many people were detained in the chaos that followed the annulment of the poll meant to have ended a decade of army rule.
His critics say Abacha intends to perpetuate military rule in a country governed by soldiers for 25 out of its 36 years of independence.
They dismiss his transition programme as a ruse for him to hang onto power, pointing to among other things the continued detention of opposition figures, including Abiola.
Further controversy was caused last year when former chief judge Mohammed Bello said Abacha was qualified to contest for the presidency, like any other Nigerian.
Up until now, Abacha had never commented on the issue despite being repeatedly urged to do so, including by members of the five political parties.

Political rallies, staged in many places around the country and beamed on state television, have labelled Abacha the messiah and suggested that he should be given a chance to continue with his programme to "sanitise" Nigeria.
Although he has stabilised the economy, reduced inflation and restored public order, the crisis unleashed by the election annulment which propelled him to power remains unresolved.
Asked in the Washington Times interview -- widely reported by the local media -- if he would run for president, Abacha said: "I have not put my mind to, never thought of it."
But he added: "It is not new in Africa, neither is it new in the sub-region, where military people have stepped into politics."
Analysts said with such comments Abacha was bound to follow the footsteps of soldiers who have seized power in Africa and then proceeded to legitimise their tenure through sham polls.
"An Abacha presidency looks like a fait accompli," said Ubani in his editorial.
But pro-democracy activists warn Abacha should not take for granted that he would have a smooth ride to the presidency.

"We are firmly opposed to the idea of General Abacha contesting under the transition programme and will continue to mobilise and educate Nigerians on the implications," said the Democratic Alternative pressure group in a statement.
